title: WHEN HONORING YOUR PASTOR BECOMES BETRAYING YOUR CONSCIENCE: THE DANGEROUS LINE BETWEEN SPIRITUAL AUTHORITY AND BLIND LOYALTY
paragraphs: WHEN HONORING YOUR PASTOR BECOMES BETRAYING YOUR CONSCIENCE: THE DANGEROUS LINE BETWEEN SPIRITUAL AUTHORITY AND BLIND LOYALTY

What happens when the person who taught you to follow Jesus begins demanding a loyalty that belongs to Jesus alone? A biblical confrontation with spiritual manipulation, misplaced devotion, wounded believers, and the freedom Christ never intended you to surrender.
There is a kind of heartbreak that happens inside a church that is difficult to explain to someone who has never experienced it.
It is not the heartbreak of losing your faith.
It is the heartbreak of discovering that someone you trusted to strengthen your faith may have been using that trust to control you.
You remember how it began.

You were struggling. Perhaps your marriage was falling apart. Perhaps guilt was eating you alive. Perhaps you had spent years running from God, and one Sunday, a sermon finally broke through the walls around your heart.
You cried.
You prayed.
You surrendered.
And somewhere in that sacred beginning, a pastor, mentor, or spiritual leader became an important part of your journey.
You respected that person.
You defended that person.
You trusted that person.
And because you believed God had used that leader to help change your life, you assumed that questioning the leader might somehow mean questioning God.
Then one day, something happened.
A decision did not seem right.
A teaching did not sound like Scripture.
Someone was mistreated, but everyone was told to remain silent.
A legitimate concern was dismissed as rebellion.
You asked a question, and instead of receiving an answer, you received a warning.
"Be careful. Don't touch God's anointed."
Suddenly, the church that once felt like a place of healing began to feel like a place where honesty was dangerous.
And a frightening question entered your mind.
If I disagree with my spiritual leader, am I disobeying God?

Stay with me, because the answer could rescue your conscience, restore your understanding of biblical authority, and perhaps help you rediscover the Jesus who never asked you to surrender your discernment to another human being.
The Bible commands believers to honor faithful spiritual leaders.
But nowhere does Scripture command believers to treat those leaders as incapable of error.
And the difference is not small.
It is the difference between shepherding and domination.
Between discipleship and dependency.
Between biblical submission and spiritual captivity.
Between following a servant of Christ and placing a servant where only Christ belongs.
Hebrews 13:17 says:
"Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account..." (KJV)
Those are serious words.
They should never be dismissed simply because authority has sometimes been abused.

God does establish leadership within His church. Pastors are not merely motivational speakers. Elders are entrusted with real responsibilities. Faithful shepherds teach, correct, protect, encourage, and care for souls.
But notice the final part of that verse.
They must give account.
Spiritual authority is not ownership.
It is stewardship under the judgment of God.

The Greek word translated "obey" in Hebrews 13:17 is πείθεσθε (peithesthe), from peithō, a verb associated with persuasion, trust, and obedience. In this context, it calls believers to respond obediently to their leaders. It does not establish unlimited obedience to every demand a leader might make.
The word translated "submit" is ὑπείκετε (hypeikete), conveying yielding or giving way.
These words describe a real posture of responsiveness toward legitimate spiritual oversight.
But they do not erase the rest of the New Testament.
They cannot be separated from the character God requires of leaders or from the supreme authority of Jesus Christ.
A pastor may deserve your respect without possessing the right to control your conscience.
An elder may provide biblical correction without possessing the right to demand unquestioning personal loyalty.
A spiritual mentor may have helped you grow without becoming the final authority over your relationship with God.
And here is where some believers have been deeply wounded.
They were taught to submit to leadership.
But they were never taught that leaders themselves must submit to Scripture.
They were taught to honor the shepherd.
But they were never taught how to recognize when a shepherd was behaving like an owner.
They were taught that rebellion is dangerous.
But they were never taught that religious authority can also become dangerous when it refuses accountability.
And sometimes, the result is devastating.
People begin hiding legitimate questions.
They silence their consciences.
They excuse patterns they would immediately recognize as wrong anywhere else.
They defend actions they know are inconsistent with the character of Christ.
Not because they stopped loving Jesus.
But because they became afraid that telling the truth might cost them their spiritual family.
Perhaps that describes you.
Perhaps you have sat in a church service with tears in your eyes, not because the Holy Spirit was convicting you of sin, but because you were terrified of what would happen if you spoke honestly.
Perhaps you watched someone leave your congregation and heard that person immediately described as rebellious, bitter, or spiritually dangerous.
Perhaps you were told that leaving a particular ministry meant leaving God's protection.
Perhaps you were pressured to give money you could not afford, surrender private information, or accept decisions that violated your conscience.
And because the person making those demands carried a Bible, you wondered whether resisting meant resisting God.
Listen carefully.
A Bible in someone's hand does not make every demand from that person's mouth biblical.
That is not disrespect toward genuine spiritual leadership.
It is respect for the authority of the Word of God.
Consider the believers in Berea.
Acts 17:11 says:
"These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so." (KJV)
Do you realize what happened?
The Bereans examined the teaching they received from the apostle Paul.
Paul.
A man personally called by Jesus Christ.
A man through whom God gave inspired apostolic teaching.
Yet the Bereans were commended for examining what they heard against the Scriptures.
The Greek expression ἀνακρίνοντες τὰς γραφὰς (anakrinontes tas graphas) describes examining or investigating the Scriptures.
They did not reject teaching merely because it challenged them.
They received it eagerly.
But they also examined it carefully.
Biblical discernment is not the enemy of biblical submission.
The Bereans demonstrated both openness and examination.
And if the Bereans were commended for testing Paul's message against Scripture, no pastor today should claim exemption from biblical examination.
Not the most popular preacher.
Not the founder of a denomination.
Not the leader of the largest congregation.
Not the minister whose sermons have reached millions.
Not even the person through whom God first brought you to repentance.
Because the authority of God's Word does not become smaller when a human personality becomes bigger.
There is another moment in Scripture that makes this even clearer.
In Galatians 2:11, Paul writes:
Peter was an apostle.
He had walked with Jesus.
He had witnessed the resurrection.
He had preached at Pentecost.
Yet when his conduct contradicted the truth of the Gospel, Paul confronted him.
Why?
Because Peter's status did not make his behavior beyond correction.
Paul's confrontation was not an attack on Christ's church.
It was a defense of Gospel truth.
Peter's behavior had compromised the implications of justification by faith and the unity of Jewish and Gentile believers in Christ.
The issue was not a minor disagreement over personal preference.
It concerned conduct that undermined the Gospel.
This distinction matters.
Not every disagreement with a pastor is evidence of abuse.
Not every difficult correction is manipulation.
Not every leadership decision requires unanimous approval.
Sometimes a faithful pastor must confront sin, and sometimes the person being corrected genuinely does need to repent.
But there is an enormous difference between a leader who opens Scripture to explain a difficult truth and a leader who uses spiritual threats to prevent that truth from being examined.
A faithful shepherd does not need to be infallible to be respected. But a shepherd who demands to be treated as infallible has crossed a dangerous line.
Now consider one of the most frequently misused phrases in conversations about church authority.
"Touch not mine anointed."
Those words appear in Psalm 105:15, referring to God's protection of His people in the historical setting described by the psalm.
The Hebrew phrase is:
אַל־תִּגְּעוּ בִמְשִׁיחָי
Al-tigge'u vimshichai.
"Touch not mine anointed." (KJV)
The word מְשִׁיחָי (meshichai) means "my anointed ones."
In the psalm's context, God is recounting His protection of the patriarchs and His covenant people.
This is not a blanket declaration that modern pastors are immune from criticism, investigation, correction, or accountability.
It is especially not permission to conceal wrongdoing.
Scripture itself establishes procedures for handling accusations against elders.
First Timothy 5:19 warns against receiving accusations against an elder without two or three witnesses.
That protects leaders from reckless allegations.
But the next verse, 1 Timothy 5:20, addresses elders who persist in sin and commands public rebuke so that others may fear.
Notice the balance.
God does not authorize careless accusations.
And God does not authorize permanent immunity.
He requires truth, fairness, evidence, and accountability.
Protecting a leader from false accusations is biblical.
Protecting a leader from the consequences of proven wrongdoing is not.
And when serious harm or criminal conduct is involved, biblical accountability must never be used as an excuse to obstruct appropriate civil reporting or protect perpetrators.
The church should be a place where truth is pursued, not buried.
Where vulnerable people are protected, not sacrificed to preserve reputations.
Where repentance is more important than image.
Where leaders understand that their calling makes them more accountable, not less.
Jesus Himself addressed the temptation to turn spiritual leadership into personal domination.
In Mark 10:42–45, He contrasted rulers who exercise authority over others with the way His disciples must lead.
His words in verse 43 are unmistakable:
"But so shall it not be among you: but whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister." (KJV)
The Greek word διάκονος (diakonos), translated "minister" in the KJV, means a servant or one who serves.
Jesus was overturning the world's obsession with status.
In His kingdom, greatness is not measured by how many people a leader can control.
It is measured by faithful service.
And Jesus did not merely teach this.
He embodied it.
The eternal Son of God washed His disciples' feet.
The One with all authority knelt before imperfect men.
The One who could command angels chose the road to Calvary.
And that contrast should trouble us.
How can someone claim to represent the crucified Servant while treating ordinary believers as personal property?
How can someone preach humility while demanding constant admiration?
How can someone proclaim freedom in Christ while making people afraid to ask honest questions?
Jesus did not die to establish a kingdom of untouchable religious celebrities.
He died to redeem sinners and reconcile them to God.
He is the Chief Shepherd.
Every earthly shepherd is accountable to Him.
First Peter 5:2–3 instructs elders to shepherd God's flock willingly and not for dishonest gain, nor as those dominating the people entrusted to them, but as examples.
The Greek expression μηδ᾽ ὡς κατακυριεύοντες (mēd' hōs katakyrieuontes) prohibits a domineering exercise of authority.
This is not a command to abandon leadership.
It is a command to exercise leadership in a manner consistent with Christ.
A faithful pastor can be firm without being cruel.
Can correct without humiliating.
Can lead without manipulating.
Can receive honor without demanding worshipful devotion.
Can admit wrongdoing without losing the dignity of the office.
And perhaps most importantly, can rejoice when believers become more dependent on Jesus rather than more dependent on the pastor.
Because the goal of Christian ministry is not to produce lifelong admirers of a preacher.
It is to make disciples of Jesus Christ.
Think about John the Baptist.
People followed him.
They listened to his preaching.
They respected his calling.
Yet when Jesus appeared, John declared:
"He must increase, but I must decrease." (John 3:30, KJV)
What a remarkable picture of spiritual leadership.
John did not panic when attention moved toward Christ.
He did not compete with Jesus for loyalty.
He understood his purpose.
He was not the Bridegroom.
He was the friend of the Bridegroom.
His joy was fulfilled when people recognized the One greater than himself.
Imagine how much healthier our churches would become if every spiritual leader carried that same conviction.
Not "How can I make these people more loyal to me?"
But "How can I help these people become more faithful to Christ?"
Not "How can I protect my reputation at all costs?"
But "How can I honor the truth even when it exposes my weaknesses?"
Not "How can I keep people afraid of leaving?"
But "How can I shepherd people so faithfully that their confidence rests in Jesus, whether or not I remain part of their lives?"
This is not weakness.
This is Christlike leadership.
And it is worth honoring.
But there is another side of this conversation that must not be ignored.
Sometimes wounded believers swing from unquestioning loyalty into unquestioning suspicion.
After experiencing manipulation, they begin assuming that every pastor is corrupt, every correction is abuse, and every church is dangerous.
That response is understandable in the aftermath of deep betrayal.
But it is not where Christ calls us to remain.
The failure of a leader does not cancel the goodness of biblical shepherding.
The misuse of authority does not mean authority itself is evil.
And the sins of some pastors must not be used to condemn faithful ministers who quietly spend their lives loving God's people.
There are pastors who visit hospital rooms when no camera is recording.
Pastors who pray over grieving families.
Pastors who counsel struggling marriages.
Pastors who faithfully preach unpopular truths because they fear God more than public opinion.
Pastors who acknowledge their mistakes.
Pastors who refuse to exploit people's generosity.
Pastors who carry burdens their congregations may never know.
These servants deserve prayer, encouragement, respect, and appropriate support.
First Thessalonians 5:12–13 calls believers to recognize those who labor among them and esteem them highly in love for their work's sake.
That is biblical honor.
But honor is not the same as surrendering moral judgment.
Love does not require pretending wrongdoing is righteousness.
Unity does not require suppressing truth.
Forgiveness does not automatically restore someone to a leadership position.
And reconciliation does not always mean returning to a relationship or institution where harm remains unaddressed.
The Gospel calls us to truth and grace together.
Not truth without compassion.
Not compassion without accountability.
Both.
Perhaps the most painful part of this subject is that spiritual manipulation often works because it attaches itself to something genuinely beautiful.
Your love for God.
Your desire to obey Scripture.
Your gratitude toward a pastor who helped you.
Your fear of becoming proud or rebellious.
Your longing to belong to a spiritual family.
These are not shameful desires.
But even good desires can be exploited when people are taught to confuse loyalty to a human leader with loyalty to Christ.
And that is why you must remember something essential.
You were purchased by the blood of Jesus Christ, not by the sacrifices of a pastor.
First Corinthians 7:23 says:
"Ye are bought with a price; be not ye the servants of men." (KJV)
In context, Paul is addressing believers' status and calling, including the realities of slavery and freedom.
It is not a command to reject all human leadership.
But its theological foundation is powerful.
Believers belong ultimately to Christ.
No human being can claim the ownership that belongs to the Redeemer.
A pastor may teach you.
A mentor may guide you.
An elder may correct you.
But only Jesus is your Savior.
Only Jesus is your Mediator in the ultimate saving sense described in 1 Timothy 2:5.
Only Jesus carried your sins to the cross.
Only Jesus conquered death.
Only Jesus is the head of His church.
And only Jesus deserves your absolute allegiance.
Now imagine a believer sitting alone in a parked car after a painful church meeting.
The engine is off.
The parking lot is almost empty.
The person has spent years serving faithfully.
Giving.
Volunteering.
Attending.
Praying.
Defending the ministry whenever someone criticized it.
But tonight, something has changed.
A question was raised.
A legitimate concern.
And instead of receiving a biblical explanation, the believer was accused of disloyalty.
The words are still ringing in their ears.
"You're becoming rebellious."
"You've lost your covering."
"God will deal with you if you oppose His servant."
The believer grips the steering wheel.
Tears fall.
And through the confusion comes a whispered prayer.
"Jesus, I don't want to rebel against You. I just want to know what is true."
If you have ever prayed something like that, hear what Scripture makes clear.
You do not have to choose between loving Jesus and examining what a leader teaches.
You do not have to call darkness light to prove your loyalty.
You do not have to surrender your conscience to demonstrate humility.
And you do not have to abandon Christ because someone who claimed to represent Him failed to reflect His character.
You can seek wise counsel.
You can examine Scripture carefully.
You can pursue appropriate accountability.
You can acknowledge your own mistakes where necessary.
You can forgive without denying the seriousness of what happened.
You can leave an unsafe or spiritually abusive environment when necessary.
And you can continue walking with Jesus.
Because the Lord who saved you is not imprisoned inside one church building, one ministry network, or one leader's approval.
This does not mean your personal interpretation is automatically correct.
We all need correction.
We all need humility.
We all need the wisdom of mature believers and the fellowship of a healthy church.
But genuine Christian community should help you grow in discernment, not train you to abandon it.
And the final test is not whether a leader makes you feel important, inspired, or afraid.
It is whether that leader's teaching and conduct remain accountable to the truth of Christ.
Jesus warned in Matthew 7:15 about false prophets who come in sheep's clothing.
He also taught that people would be recognized by their fruits.
That calls for careful discernment over time, not impulsive judgment based on rumors, personality conflicts, or isolated mistakes.
Look for patterns.
Is Scripture explained faithfully?
Are questions answered with patience?
Is financial stewardship transparent and accountable?
Are vulnerable people protected?
Can leaders acknowledge error?
Are serious allegations handled fairly and responsibly?
Is repentance expected from leaders as well as members?
Does the ministry point people toward dependence on Christ, or toward fear of displeasing a personality?
These are not questions designed to destroy the church.
They are questions that can help protect its integrity.
Because a healthy church is not one where nobody ever makes a mistake.
It is one where truth matters enough that mistakes can be acknowledged, sins can be confronted, victims can be protected, and repentance can bear genuine fruit.
And now we must bring this conversation to the place where every Christian examination belongs.
The cross.
Because this is not merely a discussion about bad leadership and good leadership.
It is a discussion about the human heart.
Leaders can become intoxicated with power.
Followers can become addicted to approval.
Entire communities can begin protecting an institution more fiercely than they protect the truth.
And every one of us can be tempted to place something created where only the Creator belongs.
That is why we need more than improved church policies.
We need the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
The cross exposes the pride that wants to dominate.
It exposes the fear that refuses to speak truth.
It exposes the idolatry that makes a human personality spiritually untouchable.
But the cross also announces mercy.
Mercy for the leader who genuinely repents of abusing authority.
Mercy for the believer who participated in a culture of silence and now chooses truth.
Mercy for the wounded Christian who has struggled to trust again.
Mercy for the person who confused a pastor's approval with God's acceptance.
At Calvary, Jesus bore the judgment sinners deserve.
Through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to those who repent and trust in Him.
And this is where the Gospel becomes more than a religious slogan.
It becomes the hope of restoration.
Not restoration through denial.
Not restoration through hiding wrongdoing.
Not restoration through forcing wounded people to pretend nothing happened.
But restoration grounded in truth, repentance, justice, mercy, and the redeeming work of Christ.
Some relationships may be reconciled.
Some leaders may be restored to fellowship while remaining disqualified from office.
Some institutions may need serious reform.
Some believers may need to find a different church where they can worship and grow safely.
The outcomes will not all look the same.
But Jesus remains faithful.
Even when people fail.
Even when churches disappoint.
Even when the person who introduced you to Christ becomes the person who makes trusting other Christians difficult.
Jesus remains who He has always been.
The Good Shepherd.
In John 10:11, He declares:
"I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep." (KJV)
Read that again.
The Good Shepherd gives His life for the sheep.
He does not treat the sheep as disposable instruments for protecting His image.
He lays down His life for them.
And if you want to understand the difference between Christlike leadership and abusive domination, begin there.
The false shepherd asks, "What can the sheep sacrifice to protect me?"
The Good Shepherd demonstrates, "I will lay down My life for the sheep."
That is the standard.
Not celebrity.
Not wealth.
Not titles.
Not charisma.
Not the size of a congregation.
Not the number of people willing to defend a leader online.
Christ.
Always Christ.
And if you are a pastor reading this, please do not hear only an accusation.
Hear an invitation.
You do not have to pretend to be perfect.
You do not have to know everything.
You do not have to win every disagreement.
You do not have to maintain an image of invulnerability.
You can be a faithful shepherd who says, "I was wrong."
You can apologize.
You can welcome appropriate accountability.
You can protect the weak.
You can correct with gentleness.
You can lead with courage.
You can point people beyond yourself to Jesus.
And in doing so, you may offer your congregation something far more valuable than the illusion of a flawless pastor.
You can show them what humble dependence on Christ looks like.
And if you are a church member reading this, honor the faithful people who shepherd you.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Support biblical ministry.
Receive correction when Scripture exposes your sin.
Do not spread unverified accusations.
Do not mistake every uncomfortable sermon for manipulation.
Do not turn a genuine wound into permission to despise the entire body of Christ.
But never forget that the greatest gift a spiritual leader can give you is not dependence on that leader.
It is a deeper love for Jesus, a stronger understanding of Scripture, and a growing maturity that helps you stand firm in the faith.
Perhaps tonight, you need to repent.
Not necessarily because you questioned a leader.
Perhaps because you have allowed bitterness to harden your heart.
Perhaps because you defended wrongdoing out of fear.
Perhaps because you made a ministry, a pastor, or even your own opinions more important than the truth of God's Word.
Or perhaps you are a leader who recognizes that you have demanded a kind of loyalty Scripture never gave you the right to demand.
Whatever the case, the answer is not to hide.
Come into the light.
First John 1:9 reminds believers that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
There is grace for the repentant.
There is hope for the weary.
There is truth for the confused.
And there is a Savior who does not need to manipulate people to keep them close.
His love is not a trap.
His lordship is not a license for human tyranny.
His grace does not excuse sin.
His truth does not abandon the wounded.
That is the Jesus we proclaim at Gospel Warrior.
And that is why our message remains:
Not because every scandal ends with an earthly happy ending.
Not because every broken relationship is repaired.
Not because every disgraced leader returns to ministry.
But because no human failure can overturn the saving power of the crucified and risen Christ.
And perhaps this message has reached you at a moment when you were considering walking away from Christianity altogether.
Please hear this before you make that decision.
The person who wounded you is not the measure of Jesus.
The church that disappointed you is not the fullness of His kingdom.
The leader who misrepresented Him does not get to define Him for you.
Look again at Christ.
Read the Gospels.
Listen to His words.
Watch how He treats the broken.
Watch how He confronts hypocrisy.
Watch how He receives repentant sinners.
Watch Him carry the cross.
And ask yourself whether the Jesus revealed in Scripture is truly the same as the distorted image someone may have given you.
You may discover that what you need to leave behind is not Jesus Christ.
It is a false understanding of what following Him requires.
And if this article has exposed something you have been carrying silently, I want to invite you into a moment of spiritual honesty.
You do not need to reveal private details or identify anyone publicly.
And if your faith has been exhausted but you refuse to give up on Jesus, simply write:
Sometimes a few honest words become the beginning of a meaningful conversation, a prayer, or an unexpected encouragement for someone who thought they were suffering alone.

And if this message brought someone to mind, consider tagging that person privately or publicly only when doing so would be welcome and helpful. Some wounds require discretion, and genuine love never needs to expose another person's pain to prove a point.
You may never know who reads it quietly.
A young believer struggling with confusion.
A pastor who needs encouragement to lead more humbly.
A church member who has been afraid to ask questions.
A family trying to rebuild its trust in Christian community.
Someone who has almost given up on Jesus because of what another person did in His name.
We also want to extend a personal invitation to those who believe this ministry is worth sustaining.
These resources are intended to help believers move beyond momentary inspiration toward deeper biblical understanding, spiritual maturity, and faithful Christian living.
But continuing and expanding this work requires time, resources, and the generosity of people who believe in the mission.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
That principle matters deeply to us.
Jesus has already accomplished what money never could.
These items can serve as reminders of biblical truth, thoughtful gifts, and practical ways to support the continuing work of the ministry.
Read.
Pray.
Grow.
Share the resources.
Encourage a struggling believer.
Keep studying Scripture.
The Gospel is not merchandise, and the grace of God is never for sale.
Our prayer is that every form of support, whether financial or otherwise, will ultimately direct attention away from ourselves and toward Jesus Christ.
Because the purpose of Gospel Warrior is not to build unquestioning loyalty to a platform, personality, or ministry.
It is to help people know, love, obey, and follow the Lord Jesus Christ.
And we must be willing to apply the very truth of this article to ourselves.
Do not accept our words merely because we speak confidently.
Examine the Scriptures.
Test what we teach.
Hold us accountable to biblical truth.
If this ministry is faithful, that examination should strengthen your confidence in Christ rather than threaten our position.
That is the kind of discipleship worth supporting.
That is the kind of faith worth passing on.
And that is the kind of spiritual maturity we pray will grow in every person this message reaches.
So tonight, whether you are a pastor, a wounded church member, a searching unbeliever, or someone who has spent years confusing human approval with divine acceptance, remember this:
Honor those who faithfully lead you.
Receive biblical correction.
Reject pride and needless division.
But never surrender the place in your heart that belongs to Jesus alone.
Because the final voice over your salvation is not the pastor who baptized you.
Not the leader who mentored you.
Not the congregation that welcomed you.
Not the institution that gave you a place to serve.
It is the Savior who died for you and rose again.
And when every human title fades, every platform disappears, and every earthly ministry reaches its end, His name will remain.
Jesus Christ.
The Shepherd who knows His sheep.
The King who does not abuse His throne.
The Redeemer who welcomes the repentant.
The Lord who is worthy of everything.
The hands that were pierced to save you are the only hands worthy of holding your ultimate allegiance.
